text: All Generation 4 coverage in Albania was taken using a “smallcam” camera, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.
NOTE: Most of the Balkans and southern Europe have Smallcam.
‘**Rifts**’ can rarely be seen in Albanian generation 3 coverage, due to poor stitching.
NOTE: Rifts are also equally common in Montenegro, and can rarely be seen in various other countries.
You can tell the three German-speaking countries apart by **camera meta **alone:

- Austria only has **Generation 3** and Generation 4 coverage (the only exceptions being Generation 2 on [one road](https://goo.gl/maps/LebHyLrqsjkqyoZMA) in Burgenland, and several [ski resort trekkers](https://goo.gl/maps/pdquUsUJoNwZghxRA)).
- Germany only has Generation 4 coverage. (the only exceptions being spills and trekkers)
- Switzerland car coverage is always [low-cam](https://goo.gl/maps/Ey7aUdEn6vc76BZc8). This can be recognized by the much bigger car blur.

Austria also has generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.
NOTE: Most of Western Europe also has smallcam.
In Generation 3 coverage, you can see two different cars:
- A white car with a [**stubby antenna**](https://goo.gl/maps/NhuDAxCVQ9TjhSUF7). There is a diagonal coil wrapped around the antenna.
- A white car with [**no antenna**](https://goo.gl/maps/nKHjWrdrmbWcUULn6).
The car’s colour is not always visible, meaning you will often see either just the stubby antenna, or no hints of the car at all.
The stubby antenna with a diagonal coil can also be found in Ecuador, Colombia, and Mexico.
The Generation 4 cars you can find in Brazil have a visible front, and have one of the following three colour patterns:
- [**Blue**](https://goo.gl/maps/cX9hiLoFAWmSxYLp8)
- [**White with a blue stripe**](https://goo.gl/maps/8m72fEE5hMYAQKF27)
- [**White**](https://goo.gl/maps/fkcFJmPtRwACz2Jv7)
Brazil also has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front.
NOTE: Brazil, Peru and Argentina are the only South American countries with smallcam.
Most of the coverage in Brazil is along the **eastern **half, with only sparse coverage in the Amazon.

It is useful for beginning players to start forming a rough mental map of where the (limited) coverage is in the western half. When you get Amazonian rounds, this can prevent you from wildly plonking hundreds of kilometres away from the nearest road.

**Area codes** are common to see in Brazil. They are often notated using parentheses, or at minimum as two separate numbers. Phone numbers are sometimes without area codes, and without them will be 8 numbers long for landline and 9 for mobile.

The pattern for each of the states is very learnable and useful. The area codes are grouped by first digit, so even just learning those can already help a lot. Notably, area codes ending in 1 will always be around major cities and state capitals.

**Postcodes (CEP) **are seen frequently on [street signs](https://goo.gl/maps/7RAf4dB5LnHm3PT36) in Brazil (though sometimes hard to read). The first two numbers will depict an area, a state or multiple states. The numbers go anti-clockwise from São Paulo, ending in Rio Grande do Sul.
**Phone numbers** can sometimes be seen underneath kilometre markers in São Paulo.
In all Generation 4 coverage in Amapá, the front right of the camera is **smudged**. In addition, all Generation 4 coverage in Amapá features the white car with the blue stripe.

The 364 through Acre is very recognisable due to the **rollercoaster-like landscape and road**: the road uniquely rides the hills rather than snaking around them. There is usually no traffic, and is covered mostly by Generation 4 blue car.

The Amazonas 319 has a very lush, bright green and tropical landscape, as it **cuts through the Amazon rainforest**. The road is flat and mostly unpaved, featuring bright orange soil. However, closer to Manaus the road becomes paved. There are wooden or ladder poles alongside the entire stretch. It is covered by the blue Generation 4 car.

The Pará section of the 163 is often **hilly, curvy, dry, and sometimes hazy**. It has a wide range of amazonian vegetation. The road is frequently trafficked, usually by transportation trucks. It is covered by the blue Generation 4 car in the north and the Smallcam car in the south.
You can often see **rifts** in Alagoas Generation 3 coverage.
Northwest Rio Grande do Sul has coverage with this **camera glitch** in Generation 3.

Canada has a fair amount of **Generation 2 coverage**, especially in rural** **or remote areas. Generation 2 can be recognized by the big circular car blur and the halo-like colour distortion in the sky.
NOTE: Generation 2 is very rare in the US. If you are between Canada and the US, and the location is in Generation 2, you are much more likely to be in Canada.
**Generation 3** is significantly more common in Canada than in the US.
In addition, the side mirrors are blurred out differently: While they generally appear as **two peaks** in Canadian Gen 3 coverage, you will mostly see a single peak in the US.

Both the US and Canada also have Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot. When the car isn’t blurred properly, you will usually see a mirror sticking out on the right side.
Rural roads in Alberta are numbered sequentially. This makes it easy to figure out your exact location using just a road sign.
- **Township roads** (Twp Rd) run east to west. Their numbers increase the more north you go.
- **Range roads** (Rge Rd) run north to south. Their numbers increase the more west you go. These numbers reset a couple of times.

[This infographic](/images/canada/canada_albertatownshipgrid.png) shows which numbers are found where. You need to multiply the numbers on the grid by 10 to get the road numbers. For example, the junction in the image example is found just north of Red Deer.
NOTE: Similarly named roads can also sometimes be seen in Saskatchewan, however they are more common in Alberta.
Rural roads in Manitoba are organised in a grid and referred to only by their number and cardinal direction.
- Roads ending in **N** run east to west. Their numbers increase by one for every mile north of the US border.
- Roads with **E** or **W** run north to south. They tell you their position relative to the principal meridian, located just west of Winnipeg.
For instance, this image was taken 105 miles north of the US border and 147 miles west of the principal meridian.
Canadian phone numbers start with a **three-digit area code**. Both landlines and mobile phones use the same area codes.
NOTE: Canadian phone numbers are formatted XXX XXX XXXX, with the area code being the first three digits. It is fairly common to see 7-digit numbers with the area code omitted.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

Costa Rica’s Generation 4 imagery was captured using a large **white pickup truck**. In many locations, it is either fully or partially visible, but can occasionally be entirely blurred out. There is an antenna attached to the front of the car.

NOTE: The Panamanian truck is almost always [fully blurred out](https://maps.app.goo.gl/SXjYfDTrfFwZTWLs8). The truck used in [Ecuador](https://maps.app.goo.gl/dSweUPGTkgTasq9B7) does not have an antenna.
Grote Berg, located in the centre of the island, can be recognised by the **stick** stuck to the front of the camera lens.

France has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.
NOTE: Most of Western Europe also has smallcam.

This guide will mainly operate with two types of administrative divisions: [**regions**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regions_of_France), totalling at **13** in European France, and **96 **[**departments**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_France), which appear on google maps as the primary administrative divisions. Other rarer divisions you may come across include [pre 2016 regions](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Map_Carte_des_Anciennes_R%C3%A9gions_2015.png/1024px-Map_Carte_des_Anciennes_R%C3%A9gions_2015.png), [historical provinces](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/France_in_1789.svg/1024px-France_in_1789.svg.png), and [regions based on cardinal directions](https://www.ffft.fr/sites/default/files/images/d%C3%A9coupage%20r%C3%A9gions%20FFFT%20et%20officielles.jpg).
Departments are often named after physical geographical features and their logos may show up on various infrastructure, shown in the next tip.
_You can practise them with [this quiz](https://geo.emily.bz/map-quiz/france/departments)._
French telephone numbers are 10 digits long, with the first two pairs of digits being two separate area codes, following two patterns:
- 01 is in Île-de-France and 02-05 goes **clockwise **from the northwest.
- 2X is in the far north, with the numbers generally increasing **anticlockwise**. 9X is an exception, being found both in the far northwest and far southeast.
Secondary area codes in Île-de-France can be seen on [this map](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/Indicatif_telephonique_IDF.jpg/1280px-Indicatif_telephonique_IDF.jpg).
NOTE: Phone numbers beginning with 06-09 are not regional.

Each department has an assigned number to it, arranged mostly [alphabetically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_France#Current_departments). This is most useful in postal codes, consisting of 5 digits, the first two representing the department they’re in.
NOTE: the same regional codes are used inside the right blue strip on [licence plates](https://maps.app.goo.gl/hdSg7fcVKbUGPcjP8).

Most departments have their own unique logo (formally called official flag), often containing stylized initials or the entire name. Notable infrastructure with department logos include [bus stops](https://maps.app.goo.gl/1CqFWtzhUqLV2k8n7), [kilometre markers](https://maps.app.goo.gl/JGY1Xwa8SvPyyV5A9), [trail banners](https://maps.app.goo.gl/kP4kjMrH3rK5gLSZ7), [directional signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/QM5gqNqrRtf4gWRR6) and [signbacks](https://maps.app.goo.gl/ZHA8UMQL6eFzSNyP6). Learning what each logo looks like is not recommended for beginners, but it can be helpful to know what they stand for when scanning.

You can find the full list of logos [here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flags_of_the_regions_of_France#French_Departments), or see them projected onto a map [here](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/06/Flag_Map_of_Departments_of_France_Version_2_%28Logo_Flags%29.png).

On rare occasions, you may find a flag attached to the antenna in the generation 3 coverage. While much of the highlighted areas has been overwritten, learning the distribution of each antenna can yield very high scores.
NOTE: All pictured colourful antenna flags are unique to France.
Generation 4 coverage in Ghana was taken using a **grey** or white **pickup truck** with an antenna in the front. The truck will be either fully or partially **blurred **most of the time.

The coverage in Ghana is **limited **and easy to memorize, as most of it was taken on its main roads and in major cities. The most dense coverage is located in the south, around the cities of Accra and Kumasi.
The majority of generation 4 coverage is close to Accra or Kumasi, with only a few major roads being covered.
Coverage in Indonesia is fairly limited. Notably, there is no coverage on Papua or adjacent islands, and coverage is sparse in areas such as Kalimantan, Aceh, Central Sulawesi and North Maluku.

The names of 2nd level subdivisions, named **‘Kabupaten’ **or **‘Kab’ **for short, translating to regency, can be found all over Indonesia on various signs and billboards. Each province is split up into multiple Kabupatens, totalling to 417 which are covered by street view, and therefore applicable in Geoguessr. These are learnable with enough time and patience.
_See the resources section for more information._

While kabupaten names appear significantly more often, a number of [signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/UgV2DtQbn4qVDL9t5) also display the **postal code**. Postal codes are five digits long and grouped by their starting digit, ranging from 1xxxx in Jakarta to 9xxxx in Maluku and Papua.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

**Generation 3 antenna** coverage is most commonly found on Java, but can very rarely be seen on Bali in and around Denpasar. It is most commonly seen in East Java, as most of the antenna coverage in the west has been overwritten by Generation 4.
Black Generation 3 coverage can be found almost everywhere in Indonesia, but is most common in **Sulawesi**.
This camera glitch, reminiscent of a **Moiré Pattern**, is found throughout Central Kalimantan.
_You can click on the image for a clearer view._
A **white **SUV with black bars and a wooden plank on the roof can rarely be seen in eastern Bali.
A **black cab** with men sitting in the truck bed can be seen near Jagasatru on Bali.

Italy has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.
Italian **area codes** follow a pattern where the first digit generally increases to the east, then south.
Each Italian region has its own unique flag.
The Campione d'Italia **exclave** in Switzerland can be recognized by its low camera, having a long antenna and a flag. There is also a body of water to the west.

NOTE: This antenna can also be found in several areas in [Switzerland](https://www.google.com/maps/@45.8917308,9.0384397,3a,38.3y,19.25h,71.73t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1s0x8K6Xn3tuFsalTznE_BGw!2e0!7i13312!8i6656).
The island of San Domino only has **overcast Generation 2** coverage, which mostly looks quite gloomy.
Kenya is mostly covered in Generation 4 **pickup truck coverage**. Most trucks are blurred out, but sometimes you can see parts of the car, which can be many different colors, or a **snorkel**.
NOTE: It is the only country other than Mongolia with a snorkel in Generation 4.
On a lot of the coverage you will see a grey Toyota SUV following the Street View car.
Generation 3 coverage in Kenya often features a **visible roof rack ** and a **snorkel**. Some Generation 3 coverage has [no visible car](https://maps.app.goo.gl/UGBAo7hH2mhLsUv46).
Upon closer inspection of signs, billboards and posters, you will notice that the **county name** is often written. Therefore, knowledge of Kenyan counties can be extremely useful in region guessing.
_You can practise Kenyan counties using the quiz in the resource section._
Most of the coverage in Kenya outside of the southwest is limited to **main roads**.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

Post codes in Kenya can be identified by [signs in the format PO BOX XXX-YYYZZ](https://maps.app.goo.gl/zkoZ8sYzmTGiRivA6), where the number YYY (usually 3 digits but sometimes 0) corresponds to a post code. This is the number which can be used to narrow down your guess. Often, the name of the city is listed after the PO BOX.
NOTE: You can sometimes see [PO BOX without the second number](https://maps.app.goo.gl/sNta3QHeJpwVVgoDA) after the hyphen which is not helpful.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it. Here is a _[quiz](https://www.super-duper.fr/quiz2024/areacodes.php?country=POST_KE&language=en&tile=gmaps&border=thin&difficulty=false&timer=false&gmaplng=en)_ to help practice Kenyan post codes_

All Generation 4 coverage in Montenegro was taken using a “smallcam” camera, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.
NOTE: Most of the Balkans and southern Europe have Smallcam.
‘**Rifts**’ can uncommonly be seen in Montenegrin generation 3 coverage, due to poor stitching.
NOTE: Rifts are also common in Albania, and can rarely be seen in various other countries.

Although rifts are common in generation 3 Montenegro coverage, coastal rounds **will almost never **have them. By the coast, there will be a [short antenna](https://goo.gl/maps/d7Fvp2NzZw37CxyFA) with no rifts. There will be a [long antenna](https://goo.gl/maps/Zpu6fUJ5o3LkTtxZ6) with rifts inland.
NOTE: An exception to this is the area around the coastal villages of Utjeha and Dobra Voda.
Within mainland Africa, Nigeria is currently the only country to have this **low-quality coverage**, known as official ari**, **or “shitcam”.

NOTE: Low quality coverage taken between 2023 and 2025 has especially [low quality](https://maps.app.goo.gl/FRmNSTEtGszBkRqEA). Often you can see huge cars through the blur, and this extremely low quality only appears elsewhere in Lebanon.

All Generation 4 coverage in North Macedonia was taken using a “smallcam” camera, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.
NOTE: Most of the Balkans and southern Europe have Smallcam.
There will **never be an antenna **on the Google car.
Every other country in Europe will have an antenna sometimes in Generation 3 coverage. For clarity’s sake: this means that cars with no antenna can be found outside North Macedonia.
NOTE: The only other country to have no antenna the majority of the time is Serbia, although there will be an antenna sometimes.
Generation 3 Coverage is **sparse**, only including some highways and some cities in the country.
The cities of Skopje, Bitola, Kumanovo, Prilep, Tetovo, Veles, Ohrid, and Strumica are the only ones with significant coverage inside the city.
You can view the official coverage in more detail on [this site](https://sv-map.netlify.app#base=roadmap&cov=official&zoom=9&center=41.4828622445409%2C22.178649902343754).
In GENERATION 3 coverage A** green truck** is visible behind the Google Car for a portion of the E-65. The truck is visible from Kichevo to Arbinovo.
NOTE: This hint is mostly obsolete
Panama was covered by a large white pickup truck that is usually **entirely blurred**. An antenna is occasionally visible.

NOTE: The [Costa Rican](https://maps.app.goo.gl/468aLVF3daz21MRLA) truck is usually unblurred. The car used in [Ecuador](https://maps.app.goo.gl/dSweUPGTkgTasq9B7) has neither an antenna nor a white metal railing.
While Panama is quite well covered, there is barely any coverage on the north coast, or east of Panama City.
The first digit of phone numbers can be used to regionguess Panama.
The numbers with a smaller font indicate potentially useful [regional two-digit codes](https://goo.gl/maps/fgoa9tJUxY5QL2C56).
NOTE: Only phone numbers with 7 digits are helpful, and any numbers starting with 5, 6, or 8 are useless as well.
The first digit of taxi and bus licence plates can be used to regionguess Panama.
NOTE: Cars travel, so they are not always reliable, especially outside of cities.
**Sunset **coverage can be found in southern Panama on a small road south of Tonosi.

Three Generation 3 Street View cars are commonly found in Russia. The two most useful ones for recognising Russia are a black and a [white](https://goo.gl/maps/MmC3SpuSmhV5ezux9) car, both with a long antenna. You may also see a [short antenna](https://goo.gl/maps/x1ryuJiJL9VjkEWx6) without a visible car.
NOTE: Short antenna without a visible car in Generation 3 is common in Europe. Both black and white cars with long antenna can show up in Generation 3 Europe, but are not as common.

The eastern half of the Kolyma Highway going to Magadan features a lot of tall **hills** and **mountains**, usually shrouded in a **haze**. Most of the roads are unpaved and feature **dark gravelly soil**. The haze is not present in the western half.
Very **hazy coverage** is found east and south of Mirny, especially along the Vilyuy river. The colour of the haze varies, but it is often orange or [white](https://goo.gl/maps/QMfuHapbJnFYAyop6).

This **forest fire haze** is found near Lake Gusinoye, southwest of Ulan-Ude in Buryatia. While similar to the haze found near [Mirny](https://maps.app.goo.gl/kZY7oWKZW3bHoFp5A), the Buryatia haze coverage can typically be recognised by the **open rolling landscape**, which is not found near Mirny.
The main road of Altai Republic has a black car long antenna driving north **through the Altai Mountains**, often with **foggy or rainy** coverage.
This is a map of Russian **area codes**. Notably, area codes starting with 8 are in the west, codes starting with 3 are fairly central and codes starting with 4 are either east or around Moscow.
This is the full coverage map of Russia. It can be helpful to know areas where there isn’t any coverage. The coverage is notably very sparse in the east and north.
You can check out the extent of the official coverage[ on this website](https://sv-map.netlify.app/#base=roadmap&cov=official&zoom=4&center=63.09475846224108%2C101.77734375000001).

[White car long antenna](https://maps.app.goo.gl/szUNXBWMYPjJ6jMA6) is found in many places, most commonly in [southern Chelyabinsk](https://maps.app.goo.gl/u2ofsEtYhTK1kxpr9), on [snow coverage around Novosibirsk](https://goo.gl/maps/WT1mwvr1mZH9Nsy88), and in the [Far East](https://maps.app.goo.gl/UcNfar31Lf4yD8pD7) beginning in [Amur Oblast](https://maps.app.goo.gl/uJivjvnTnNdf4LHq5).

NOTE: While [Kamchatka](https://goo.gl/maps/vbKvMrHXtE7anj636) technically has a silver car (with a B type antenna), it often appears white and is part of the small group of exceptions to black and white.

The [A-type short antenna](https://maps.app.goo.gl/13hZAJw2TiAoyFP17) has its highest ridge on the right. Notable areas for this antenna are around [Kaluga](https://maps.app.goo.gl/JvchV2vn13QwiTG57), [Orenburg](https://maps.app.goo.gl/nYa3htnmJtm9RUEc9), and [Krasnodar](https://maps.app.goo.gl/48JHYVMTGEwN7XCu8).

The [B-type short antenna](https://maps.app.goo.gl/otoKbscwAem4eCh89) has its highest ridge on the left. This antenna is wide-ranging, but it is most notably found near [Nizhny Novgorod](https://maps.app.goo.gl/6nmWkEgaUkHRydZt5), [Elista](https://maps.app.goo.gl/sb6XLo7VMBzFQiiu8), and [Yekaterinburg](https://maps.app.goo.gl/3VHAgPgQ6EWcbjys8) and [Tyumen](https://maps.app.goo.gl/rcYGf1PeEnWmD1Sc6).

The [B-type pronounced antenna](https://maps.app.goo.gl/WwzMFjRSbmQUgBHB9) is the same as the B-type antenna but the ridge is more “rectangular”. This antenna is fairly limited, only being found commonly in [Moscow Oblast](https://maps.app.goo.gl/tziG6gD8RNd8ByJN8), [Kurgan Oblast](https://maps.app.goo.gl/HMFY2AUsYsPMmEFm6), [near Krasnoyarsk](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Wv94BFV16DXcfnVx6), and [southwest Krasnodar](https://maps.app.goo.gl/9hM7GWG3Mk7AazpJ7).

The [C-type short antenna](https://maps.app.goo.gl/7WisPoWqAk3itE7eA) can be thought of as a low A-type or a “twisting antenna” with the ridges being further from the top. It is found [north](https://maps.app.goo.gl/snkxCqnaS1bZc1hY9) and [east](https://maps.app.goo.gl/6gMAwy8bad7C9J2dA) of Moscow, with the furthest south being [Rostov Oblast](https://maps.app.goo.gl/GjFfAVgNQaRzLKkL7).

The [blurred short antenna](https://maps.app.goo.gl/8uWV4EHvPCH1dZKUA) is visibly blurrier than any of the other short antennas. It is mainly found in two major clusters around [Ufa](https://maps.app.goo.gl/rgZgng4EcRjznQuP6) and from [Stavropol](https://maps.app.goo.gl/7d5Q8kbPNPQPDMuGA) to [Makhachkala](https://maps.app.goo.gl/ujH4F6CZZc3qeSRN7).

The [A-type long antenna](https://maps.app.goo.gl/PuGiesP9DAUdSiRKA) has its highest ridge on the right side. Notable areas include [Leningrad Oblast](https://maps.app.goo.gl/4GDjJxHqF2cerU1RA), [Republic of Karelia](https://maps.app.goo.gl/MN3ZHGme7BvopS7h9), and [Vologda Oblast](https://maps.app.goo.gl/KRnogy4K1mUbL9y99). Almost all the white car long antenna coverage is A-type, so checking for A-type can also help confirm car colour.

The [B-type long antenna](https://maps.app.goo.gl/xiJHmjsXcMQyQZ1d9) has its highest ridge on the left side. Notable areas include [Yaroslav](https://maps.app.goo.gl/ZdC9XJiP3NKKA9QA6) to [Vladimir](https://maps.app.goo.gl/wEscjWspwirDVd696), [Tula Oblast](https://maps.app.goo.gl/ajNom88LdYrKfRAX6), and much of the coverage near [Tuva](https://maps.app.goo.gl/icUb6qp4Y8MzFd2P7) and [Irkutsk](https://maps.app.goo.gl/UmZN7hTvhWZv6yKk8).

NOTE: There are two other long antenna types, referred to as [CA](https://maps.app.goo.gl/eMwfHi2kLMyXc8u27) and [CB](https://maps.app.goo.gl/tDHKLKq8ENnxfWKEA), but due to their relative lack of usefulness they will not be covered here.

[Blurred long antenna](https://maps.app.goo.gl/uqSetFHbhpcz8xoy9) is visibly blurrier than other long antenna cars, and is a strong clue for [Sakhalin](https://maps.app.goo.gl/NZW6zaBoyGu7Wn6u7) and [various](https://maps.app.goo.gl/zcueGiDZjMNgD5PZA) [roads](https://maps.app.goo.gl/UyHPvXwew65N9W1C8) in the east, as well as much of [Khanty-Mansi](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Vpwb7fPXkVYdxHmYA). On the other end there exists a blurred antenna in far western [Bryansk Oblast](https://maps.app.goo.gl/nKJyHgpuCi95BtWu7) and some of [Tula Oblast](https://maps.app.goo.gl/44N5R9CyPjxWu2RL9).

The [tilted short antenna](https://maps.app.goo.gl/9dsW6TyNZJ1vTVo69) is visibly tilted to the left and can be found primarily on a diagonal from [St. Petersburg](https://maps.app.goo.gl/uYJumDRfPtDcYF8i7) down to [Volgograd](https://maps.app.goo.gl/HcLrcfJw396hVA3k6), with exceptions in [Stavropol](https://maps.app.goo.gl/xnVy4Amy7TYgydFG6) and [Ufa.](https://maps.app.goo.gl/3ndyQtC4AoWqDXns5) Since the ridge is on the same side, it can sometimes appear as the A-type short antenna.
A large, red brake light is common in Kaliningrad, however it can also be found in some [older coverage](https://goo.gl/maps/bms7QA2bzAr5VLBX8) in western Russia.
Autumn Generation 3 coverage is common in Kaliningrad, Bryansk, Tula, and Belgorod in western Russia, but Kaliningrad only has autumn coverage.
In Generation 4 coverage, **significant snow on the ground** is most commonly seen in Saratov Oblast and Eastern Voronezh Oblast.

**Generation 4** coverage is quite extensive and is found in most federal subjects in the country. Notably, areas like the Altai mountains and most of the Far East lack Generation 4 completely. Knowing where Generation 4 can be found isn’t the most helpful at the beginner level; other clues like season and car are more important. The dark red signifies areas where all of the coverage is Generation 4.

[Winter Generation 4](https://maps.app.goo.gl/tKFTbt1t6mYGmF1CA) is most common in the south of Russia, ranging from [Ryazan](https://www.google.com/maps/@54.521468,41.2920492,3a,75y,136.68h,90.82t,1.58r/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1s8GGSJc8bRgrChfct0st5lg!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) all the way down to [Kabardino-Balkaria](https://maps.app.goo.gl/sqbQHZkc1aXttg8G9) and [Dagestan](https://maps.app.goo.gl/eSpNpPM7VYWquBPN7). Winter can appear differently depending on the month (and even time of month the coverage was taken) which can be used to further regionguess.

[Spring Generation 4](https://maps.app.goo.gl/mxR9jx12qcpoqiX47) is common in several distinct places, such as around [Kemerovo](https://maps.app.goo.gl/AYpeDSAXjY4DTcfHA) and [Krasnoyarsk](https://maps.app.goo.gl/6XmSQBo12yhE4peS7), [Orenburg](https://maps.app.goo.gl/gGk8Qr7GFamJkEUj9) and [Kamyshin](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Xzo5rBpi1mDngfmw7), around [Lipetsk](https://maps.app.goo.gl/5rDYMi3imMh6wZ9S6), and in [Moscow city](https://maps.app.goo.gl/CzcoMF9KbXZqerCWA). Differentiating these places typically comes down to landscape, as they tend to be fairly distinct.

[Summer Generation 4](https://maps.app.goo.gl/87VXQczGm3HeChX18) is the most common coverage in generation 4. It is pretty much everywhere except in the south and some of the east, but can be further subdivided by car colour.

[Autumn Generation 4](https://maps.app.goo.gl/4ePdHYjvkycsZWMP6) is quite rare and only found around [Kazan](https://maps.app.goo.gl/CuYMZ5RFdFKH4CFX7) and a few roads in [Murmansk](https://maps.app.goo.gl/FVbne7gzizSc2mdu8), as well as some of [Ulan-Ude](https://maps.app.goo.gl/cGxwLd6k866DgMRr9).

[Generation 4 red car](https://maps.app.goo.gl/XZNnHtvtZbyWYqt99) is the most common generation 4 car meta, found primarily east around [Khanty-Mansi](https://maps.app.goo.gl/urkHYCZryyhY8kxdA), as well as along the main highways down to [Irkutsk](https://maps.app.goo.gl/xm2khKQjsmjipnq9A) and [Ulan-Ude](https://maps.app.goo.gl/camcQ4mEZpFN61Um9). There is also a sizable patch near [Penza](https://maps.app.goo.gl/V1cagu4DLNtD9pGq5) and [Tatarstan](https://maps.app.goo.gl/vitVoMssWGjKgixL6), as well as [Rostov-on-Don](https://maps.app.goo.gl/YCTYFcj5NZ1efTRN9).

[Generation 4 white car](https://maps.app.goo.gl/ysyGKt4TvtWbGAHC7) is found in the May coverage near [Lipetsk](https://maps.app.goo.gl/FS32oVQjxE4G5bu57), in [Moscow city](https://maps.app.goo.gl/YtkYaj1V3t1P5nqk9), and most notably across all the coverage north of Berkatit in the [Sakha Republic](https://maps.app.goo.gl/vE7pUiAVqX3rvTAg7) and [Magadan](https://maps.app.goo.gl/AGFGntoW6UFFcPm79).

[Generation 4 black car](https://maps.app.goo.gl/hV1BDavTfgWjBezk8) is found mostly near [Moscow](https://maps.app.goo.gl/d3GSjMCXAaZiwfBp9), [Tver](https://maps.app.goo.gl/UqwBFR7gry7wDpZy9), and [Voronezh](https://maps.app.goo.gl/p5YktDMBB7Mksd8SA), with some also existing in [Tatarstan](https://maps.app.goo.gl/w6tJLmTsuvTsMHvJ6) and less commonly in the south.
All the coverage in Rwanda is made with a Generation 4 camera. In most of the coverage, the Google car is a pickup truck which will be covered entirely by a **big blur**.
Sometimes the Google car is entirely visible: it is a big **white **or **brown pickup truck** with a brakelight. The camera mount is visible.
The coverage has a noticeable **hazy tint** to it, which is especially apparent in the sky.
NOTE: In Africa, similar hazy Generation 4 coverage is common in Senegal.
Rwanda has **quite limited coverage**: street view is limited to Kigali, and a couple of other patches elsewhere in Rwanda.

Serbia has **4 different truck colours** that were used in different areas.

Serbia also has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot. And a short antenna or black blur can be seen on the backside.
NOTE: Most of the Balkans also have Smallcam.
Most of the generation 3 coverage in Serbia was taken by a Google car with **no antenna**.
NOTE: Other than North Macedonia, almost all of central and eastern Europe has antenna coverage in Generation 3.
This is a generation 3 coverage map of Serbia. Most of the coverage is in the north in Vojvodina, around Belgrade and in the southeast around Niš. Kosovo does not have any coverage.

Serbia uses 2 digit area codes, with the first digit **between 1 and 3**. Area codes starting with 2 are found in the north, area codes starting with 1 are found in central and eastern Serbia. Area codes starting with 3 are found in the south-west.
Generation 3 **Fall coverage** can be seen in this region south of Čačak, and a small area around Valjevo.
A white Google Car with a **short antenna** can be seen in Novi Sad, Kovilj, in and around Belgrade, Niš, and the E75 connecting them.
NOTE: The white car is not always visible.
A **grey pickup truck** can be found in some Generation 4 coverage.

NOTE: Similar pickup trucks can also be found in a few other countries. Most relevantly in [Georgia](https://maps.app.goo.gl/x7eAbxAkPQHsJFEZ8) but it is also found in [Senegal](https://maps.app.goo.gl/qVLNzZSjP3uTWXcg8), [Rwanda](https://maps.app.goo.gl/XAwvwbthLQEbbY1n8), [Kenya](https://maps.app.goo.gl/ggiEBc94DWL7BQwp7), [Ghana ](https://maps.app.goo.gl/LN64SQFrKaRJLLoaA)and [Paraguay](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Yyuyeus81T3fYH9k8).
**Generation 2** coverage is **rare** in the US. If you have a Generation 2 location in a North American setting, you are more likely to be in Canada.
The exception to this is Alaska, and to a lesser extent Hawaii, which have a fair amount of Generation 2. You can also rarely see Generation 2 in rural areas of the Deep South.
**Generation 3** coverage is also significantly less common than in Canada.

In addition to having less Generation 3 coverage than Canada, the side mirrors are also blurred out differently: While they generally appear as two peaks in Canadian Gen 3 coverage, you will mostly see a **single peak** in the US.

**Generation 3** coverage in the US and Canada generally has **no visible antenna**. This can be helpful to distinguish it from Europe in low-info rounds. Some European Generation 3 coverage has no visible antenna, but most of it does.

There is an important exception: in national parks in the US, you can find a Generation 3 car with a [stubby antenna](https://goo.gl/maps/6nngRLvsmvVm7SPS8) with diagonal coils around it. Still, this specific type of antenna is not found in Europe.

Both the US and Canada also have Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot. When the car isn’t blurred properly, you will usually see a mirror sticking out on the right side.

**Interstate Highways** are divided highways that often span large areas of the United States. Even-numbered Interstates run west to east, with the lowest numbers along the Gulf Coast and Mexico border. Odd-numbered highways run south to north, with the lowest numbers along the West Coast.

**US Highways** are also typically long roads that are sometimes (but not always) divided. The numbering system is generally the inverse of Interstate Highways, with low odd-numbered highways located along the East Coast and low even-numbered highways located close to the Canadian border in the north of the country.
NOTE: There are generally more exceptions to the US Highway numbering system than the Interstate Highway numbering system, in terms of placement.

As part of a promotional campaign, the TransAmerica Trail from Oregon to North Carolina was covered by a **Ford Bronco**. The car can be recognised by its unblurred black roof and red hood, and is mostly found on unpaved rural roads.
Looking [backwards](https://maps.app.goo.gl/Zb8pFNSX2FFoRmK98), you will see two other Ford SUVs escorting the camera car.
